definition: Weak supervision (also known as semi-supervised learning) is a paradigm in machine learning, the relevance and notability of which increased with the advent of large language models due to the large amount of data required to train them.
details: It is characterized by using a combination of a small amount of human-labeled data (exclusively used in more expensive and time-consuming supervised learning paradigm), followed by a large amount of unlabeled data (used exclusively in unsupervised learning paradigm). In other words, the desired output values are provided only for a subset of the training data. The remaining data is unlabeled or imprecisely labeled. Intuitively, it can be seen as an exam and labeled data as sample problems that the teacher solves for the class as an aid in solving another set of problems. In the transductive setting, these unsolved problems act as exam questions. In the inductive setting, they become practice problems of the sort that will make up the exam.

explainer.lead: Weak supervision (also called semi-supervised learning) combines a small amount of human-labeled data with a large amount of unlabeled or imprecisely labeled data. Its relevance increased with large language models because of the large amount of data required to train them.

tiers.eli5: It is like studying with a few worked examples and then practising on many unsolved problems to learn the rest.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers label a small subset and let the model learn from the much larger unlabeled remainder. The pitfall is that imprecise labels can propagate error.
tiers.paperLevel: A paradigm in which desired output values are provided only for a subset of the training data, the rest being unlabeled or imprecisely labeled. Intuitively, labeled data are sample problems for an exam.

explainer.example: An exam analogy: a few sample problems are labeled, and the learner generalizes to the many unlabeled questions.
